bib.title: VeriHarness: Scaling Agentic Verification for Long-Horizon Tasks

legacy_report:
SOURCE: VeriHarness: Scaling Agentic Verification for Long-Horizon Tasks. Caiqi Zhang (Cambridge; work done as a Google Cloud AI Research intern), Rujun Han, Zifeng Wang, Zoey CuiZhu, Nigel Collier (Cambridge), Tomas Pfister, Chen-Yu Lee (Google Cloud AI Research). arXiv 2610.00972v1, cs.AI, 1 Oct 2026 (header date 2026-10-02). Preprint, no venue.

COVERAGE: All 28 pages, 89,657 chars, read in full. This includes appendices A-K, tables and the reference list (skimmed). Figures were read from the extracted text and captions only, not rendered. I did not run the figures script.

CORE CLAIM: The generator's own model, given a workspace, evidence tools and skills, can verify its own long-horizon artifacts better than judge or vote methods. It works from N=10 rollouts of the same model and has no reference answers or rubrics. A "disagreement resolver" tests disputed claims against environment evidence. A separate "consensus challenger" hunts for shared errors and omitted requirements. A fresh-context adjudicator then selects a base rollout and writes a revision plan.

HEADLINE NUMBERS (Table 2)
- Setup: 5 benchmarks (APEX-Agents v1.0 480 tasks, Workspace-Bench Lite 100, WorkBuddy 200, SpreadsheetBench 2 321, JobBench 65). Models are Gemini 3.5 Flash and Claude Opus 4.8, each as both generator and verifier, thinking "high". Every method gets the same frozen pool of 10 rollouts per task. Scores are the mean of 3 verifier runs, each benchmark on its native scale, and the average is unweighted.
- Selection only: +4.4 points over a single rollout with Flash (47.2 to 51.6) and +4.1 with Opus (49.6 to 53.7).
- With revision: +6.2 with Flash (53.4) and +6.4 with Opus (56.1).
- Opus on APEX-Agents: 35.8 to 47.5 (+11.7).
- Baselines (average): Flash majority vote 47.5, best-of-N judge 47.3, pairwise tournament 49.1, LLM-as-a-Verifier 49.5, agentic verifier with env. access and no protocol 49.4. The selection oracle is 62.7 (Flash) and 63.1 (Opus).
- The agentic verifier with environment access but no protocol or skills "recovers only about half of the harness's gain".
- Pool analysis (Fig 2, APEX-Agents, Opus, 10-rollout pools, 1,692 claims): 34% of consensus values are wrong (n=917). Disputed claims (n=775) have a correct candidate 74% of the time, but the most frequent value is right only 47% of the time.
- Cost (App K): Selection costs $1.44 per task with Flash and $3.92 with Opus. Revision adds about 3x that. This is verifier cost only, at list price, with 86-91% of input tokens cached. Without the cache discount, selection costs $5.40 (Flash) and $13.06 (Opus). Several baselines' costs are estimates, not metered.
- The authors release about 26,000 rollouts, generated at a cost of over $100,000.

ABLATIONS (Table 4, full harness with revision, 3-seed means)
- Opus average: resolver only 54.3, challenger only 52.6, both 56.1, no skills 53.8, single context 55.3. Single rollout is 49.6.
- Flash: resolver only 51.5, challenger only 50.0, no skills 51.3, single context 52.6, full 53.4. Single rollout is 47.2.
- Merging the two investigations into one context costs 0.8 points (Opus) and 0.8 points (Flash).
- Selection gain by pool entropy (APEX-Agents, Opus): +0.6 on 154 unanimous pools, +6.1 on 262 disputed pools. The gain rises from +4.5 (low entropy) to +7.7 (medium), and the +9.4 figure is the high-entropy bucket of only 15 pools.
- Aggregating the pool into a new artifact without evidence stays below the harness on every benchmark: 49.9 vs 53.4 (Flash) and 52.3 vs 56.1 (Opus).
- Portability: running the protocol inside Gemini CLI, Claude Code or Codex keeps most of the gain. With Opus, it falls back to single-rollout level on JobBench, and Claude Code does the same on SpreadsheetBench 2.

SELF-EVOLVING SKILLS (Fig 4)
- Setup: Opus on APEX-Agents and SpreadsheetBench 2, held-out subsets, about 75/25 dev/held-out split.
- Evolving from an empty library (condition C) improves held-out score by +11.0 on APEX and +5.7 on SB-2.
- Evolving from the human library (condition D) adds +6.8 on APEX and +3.7 on SB-2 over the human library (B). Final scores: APEX A 38.6, B 45.3, C 49.6, D 52.1; SB-2 A 32.8, B 35.7, C 38.5, D 39.4.
- Only one run and no significance tests: "The figures report point estimates and do not establish statistical significance."

QUOTES
- p.2: "consensus does not guarantee correctness, while disagreement between rollouts can expose correct alternatives."
- p.10: "The verifier tends to stop where the rollouts stopped, and telling it where else to look requires prior knowledge of how artifacts fail". In about 70% of the shared errors that survived the challenger, it had checked an intermediate result that was correct while the error sat in a later step (Table 7).
- p.11: "its self-checks are mostly confirmatory (Long et al., 2026)", and "a model cannot correct its own reasoning without external feedback (Huang et al., 2024)". These are the related-work findings the authors set out to get around.
- p.7: "so access alone is not sufficient."

LIMITS / NOT SHOWN
- The authors concede the cost of generating 10 rollouts, no per-rollout scalar score, same-model only (no stronger verifier tested), and added latency.
- Every benchmark is a document, spreadsheet or code-patch workspace task. The paper does not test open-ended tasks without source files, or tasks without a rollout pool.
- The comparison is against the single-rollout mean, not against a cheaper single-pass self-check or a retry loop.
- Seed spread is shown, but there are no confidence intervals or significance tests.
- Graders are mostly LLM judges (Gemini 3 Flash, an Opus agent-as-judge), so judge bias is possible.
- The evolution experiments use development-set grader feedback. The paper says generalization "beyond these task distributions, and improvement without development grader feedback, remain to be established".
- The skill library is human-authored, and the "without skills" ablation costs 2.3-2.6 average points.
- The paper does not address termination criteria, loop detection or retry taxonomy.

BUILDS ON
- Self-consistency (Wang et al., ICLR 2023) and Universal Self-Consistency (Chen et al., 2023).
- LLM-as-a-judge (Zheng et al., NeurIPS 2023).
- Repeated sampling (Brown et al., "Large Language Monkeys", 2024).
- LLM-as-a-Verifier (Kwok et al., 2026), as the prior best baseline.
- Mixture-of-Agents aggregation (Wang et al., ICLR 2025).
- Agent-as-a-judge (Zhuge et al., ICML 2025).
- Skill and experience libraries (Voyager, Wang et al., TMLR 2024; ReasoningBank, Ouyang et al., ICLR 2026).
- Expected information gain (Lindley, 1956).
- Scalable oversight (Bowman et al., 2022).
- Debate (Irving et al., 2018).

FIT TO NOTE 05-verification-loops.md
- Best fit is the "separating generation from evaluation" section. The paper shows an independent verifier context with tool and environment access beats judge-only checking, and the evidence-record structure is a concrete example.
- Secondary fits are asymmetric QA and "when a verifier is worth deleting". Selection gain is about zero (+0.6) when the pool is unanimous, which says when a verifier adds little. There is also a self-verification angle: the paper cites others' findings that self-checks are confirmatory, and its own result is that the same model needs an evidence-grounded protocol plus skills.
- It does not fit the three-layer termination check, definition of done, loop detection or retry taxonomy.
- Overall it is moderately relevant. It is a best-of-N verification paper, not an in-loop verification paper. The "sharpens" case is a separation and evidence claim, not the termination or retry material.

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Figure 3 (p.4), a worked example in which a resolver finds the draft file superseded by the final one and a challenger in a separate context catches the shared USD/EUR error. It shows both checking roles and the fresh-context adjudicator at a glance. Figure 2 (p.2) is the alternative, for the 34% wrong-consensus statistic.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. The extraction is clean apart from run-together words in some places. Figures were not rendered.
